paragraphs: The paper studies adversarial training in a setting where reliability matters more than average performance. Its testbed is a language generation task that aims to avoid descriptions involving injuries. A generator proposes text completions, and a classifier filters them. The researchers develop several ways to find failures in that classifier, including a tool that helps human adversaries search.

The approach turns discovered failures into training material. In this task, the researchers also find that very conservative filtering thresholds can be used without significantly reducing output quality. This matters because stricter filtering would be less useful if it removed too many acceptable completions.

Adversarial training makes attacks of the kinds used during training harder to find, while preserving performance on ordinary inputs. Human search takes three times longer without tools; with the assistance tool, it increases from 13 to 26 minutes. These results demonstrate increased resistance to the tested attacks, rather than establishing that catastrophic failures are impossible. The authors identify stronger attack tools and better measurements of high reliability as directions for further work.
neurips-2022-adversarial-training-for-hi.tldr: Adversarial training makes failures harder to find in a text-filtering testbed without reducing ordinary-task performance.

paragraphs: The paper addresses controlling a stochastic linear system when its dynamics are unknown and mistakes incur quadratic costs. A controller must learn the system while choosing actions. The authors revisit Reward-Biased Maximum Likelihood Estimation, or RBMLE, which modifies parameter estimation to favor models associated with larger rewards.

Their algorithm connects this approach with Upper Confidence Bound methods. It combines RBMLE's penalty with UCB's constraints, bringing together two ways of making optimistic decisions under uncertainty. The theoretical result is regret growing on the order of the square root of the time horizon. The abstract identifies this as the best known rate for the problem, so the combination preserves a strong existing guarantee.

The empirical evidence comes from extensive simulations involving real-world system examples, including Boeing 747 and unmanned aerial vehicle flight control. Augmented RBMLE substantially outperforms UCB, Thompson Sampling, and StabL in those studies. Its advantage is smaller against Input Perturbation and moderate against Randomized Certainty Equivalence. These comparisons distinguish a shared theoretical growth rate from the practical performance differences observed in the simulated control problems.
neurips-2022-augmented-rbmle-ucb-approac.tldr: Combining reward-biased estimation with UCB constraints preserves square-root regret and improves simulated adaptive-control performance.

paragraphs: In this bandit setting, each available arm has an average reward drawn from an unknown distribution. Sampling an arm produces noisy evidence about its average. Instead of concentrating only on the best arm, the paper asks how many observations are needed to estimate broader properties of that distribution, including its mean, median, maximum, and trimmed mean.

The authors compare offline estimation with an online setting where the learner can repeatedly decide whether to investigate a new arm or sample an existing one again. This flexibility does not improve the sample complexity of estimating the mean. It does significantly reduce the observations needed for several other properties, showing that the value of adaptive sampling depends on the quantity being estimated.

The paper supplies general algorithmic frameworks for both settings and matching lower bounds based on Wasserstein distances, establishing optimal sample complexities. For median estimation, it also identifies a noise-dependent threshold phenomenon concerning when Gaussian-smoothed distributions become indistinguishable. This connects a particular estimation challenge to the broader question of how noise hides differences between distributions.
neurips-2022-beyond-the-best-distributio.tldr: Adaptive sampling improves optimal estimation costs for several reward-distribution properties, but offers no advantage for estimating the mean.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how successive regions of the brain's ventral visual pathway represent images. Traditional experiments with carefully designed stimuli reveal important properties, but their conclusions are shaped by the hypotheses used to choose those stimuli. The authors instead train encoding models solely to predict functional MRI responses, then examine the visual representations those models acquire.

The models generalize strongly to artificial stimuli and new datasets. Models trained to predict responses in ventral-occipital and lateral-occipital regions also reproduce complex visual behaviors, including object categorization and human judgments of image similarity. Models targeting early visual regions do not show the same result. The distinction links the training target within the visual pathway to the kinds of behavior the learned representation can support.

Further analysis probes biases in the models' representations and produces hypotheses that can be tested experimentally. The findings suggest an emphasis on shape along the ventral stream and offer a common account of several previously studied neural phenomena. The contribution is a response-driven route to investigating visual processing, with models serving as tools for generating and organizing scientific hypotheses.
neurips-2022-characterizing-the-ventral-.tldr: Models trained only to predict brain responses reveal region-specific visual representations and suggest shape-based processing along the ventral stream.

paragraphs: Text generation often needs to satisfy requirements beyond producing fluent sentences. Some requirements are hard constraints, such as including specified keywords. Others are softer preferences, such as fitting surrounding text or expressing a particular style. The paper introduces COLD, a decoding framework that brings these different requirements into a shared mathematical formulation.

COLD represents constraints through an energy function and uses gradient-based sampling with Langevin dynamics to reason over them. This makes the constraints part of the generation procedure. The framework can be applied directly to existing language models that generate from left to right, without training a separate task-specific version of the model.

The authors demonstrate the approach on generation with required words, abductive reasoning, and counterfactual reasoning. Across these applications, both automatic measurements and human assessments support its effectiveness. The contribution is therefore a flexible way to control generation through the decoding process itself. Its unifying formulation matters because the same framework accommodates different kinds of requirements, rather than requiring each application to be handled through its own fine-tuned language model.
neurips-2022-cold-decoding-energy-based-.tldr: COLD uses energy functions and gradient-based sampling to guide existing language models through text-generation constraints without task-specific fine-tuning.

paragraphs: The paper studies decisions made under uncertainty when contextual information is also available. Its central question is how that context should shape the uncertainty considered during optimization. The authors use Conditional Robust Optimization, where the set of possible disturbances depends on the information associated with a particular decision.

Their framework jointly learns a partition of the contextual data space and constructs a deep uncertainty set for each partition. In plain terms, it learns both which contexts should be grouped together and what uncertainty should be represented within each group. Learning these pieces together makes the uncertainty description responsive to context, rather than using one description across all cases.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for uncertainty-set coverage and the resulting value-at-risk performance. These address whether the sets capture uncertain outcomes and how the optimization performs according to a risk criterion. Experiments with simulated and real-world data illustrate the method and compare it with two approaches that do not use context. The comparisons demonstrate the value of incorporating contextual information into robust decision-making.
neurips-2022-data-driven-conditional-rob.tldr: Jointly learning context groups and their uncertainty sets supports robust decisions with coverage and value-at-risk guarantees.

paragraphs: Mean-field games describe many agents whose individual decisions interact with the behavior of a large population. This paper targets a difficult version of that problem: the solver may lack derivatives of the interaction preferences, and the population must reach a specified final distribution exactly. Together, these requirements challenge many numerical methods.

The authors generalize the Schrödinger bridge, an entropy-regularized model of transporting distributions, to incorporate mean-field interactions. They use forward-backward stochastic differential equations to derive a computational framework resembling temporal-difference learning. That connection allows techniques from deep reinforcement learning to support practical training. They also show that their objective provides necessary and sufficient conditions for the mean-field problem.

The resulting method, DeepGSB, outperforms prior approaches on classical population-navigation problems. It also solves an opinion-depolarization problem with 1,000 dimensions. These findings demonstrate both the method's performance on established examples and its ability to tackle a high-dimensional application. The broader contribution is a bridge between population-level interaction models, distribution transport, and learning procedures that can make demanding mean-field problems computationally accessible.
neurips-2022-deep-generalized-schrodinge.tldr: DeepGSB extends Schrödinger bridges to difficult mean-field games and demonstrates a solver for a 1,000-dimensional opinion-depolarization problem.

paragraphs: The paper formalizes reward hacking: improving an imperfect proxy objective can worsen performance on the objective that actually matters. It calls a proxy unhackable when an increase in expected proxy return can never cause a decrease in expected true return. This is a strong ordering requirement across the policies being considered.

The authors examine whether simplifying a reward can meet that requirement, for example by dropping terms or ignoring small distinctions between outcomes. Their analysis shows that these intuitive strategies usually do not suffice. Because reward is linear in state-action visit counts, unhackability is highly restrictive. Across all stochastic policies, the abstract states that an unhackable pair requires at least one reward function to be constant.

The picture changes when attention is restricted to deterministic policies or finite collections of stochastic policies. Nontrivial unhackable pairs then always exist, and the paper gives necessary and sufficient conditions for reward simplifications. The results make the policy set central to understanding reward gaming. They also expose a tension between specifying a narrow task through a simplified reward and preserving alignment with a broader objective.
neurips-2022-defining-and-characterizing.tldr: A formal analysis shows that preventing reward gaming imposes strong restrictions that depend on which policies are considered.

paragraphs: Visual models trained with language supervision can transfer to many tasks, but comparing that transfer fairly requires consistent evaluation procedures. ELEVATER addresses this problem with a benchmark and toolkit for pretrained language-augmented visual models. Its evaluation suite includes 20 image-classification datasets and 35 object-detection datasets, each supplemented with external knowledge.

The toolkit automates hyperparameter tuning to support fairer model adaptation. This matters because comparisons can reflect how carefully each model was adapted as well as the quality of its pretrained representation. The authors also introduce initialization methods that use language information and report significant improvements in adaptation performance.

ELEVATER evaluates transfer from several perspectives. Zero-shot and few-shot settings examine performance with no task examples or only a small number, while linear probing and full fine-tuning examine different levels of parameter adaptation. Together, these settings make it possible to compare how models use labeled data and how much adaptation they require. The paper's contribution is a common evaluation framework that connects broad task coverage with practical tools for adapting and comparing models.
neurips-2022-elevater-a-benchmark-and-to.tldr: ELEVATER combines diverse visual tasks, automated tuning, and multiple adaptation settings to benchmark language-augmented visual models.

paragraphs: Selecting useful input features becomes difficult when a task provides only a few labeled examples. The paper addresses this scarcity by learning from labeled data across multiple related tasks. The goal is to use that shared experience to choose relevant features for a target task with little supervision.

The method measures dependence between each feature and the label using the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, a kernel-based measure. Rather than fixing the kernels in advance, neural networks construct them using the few labeled examples available for a task. This lets the dependence measure incorporate task-specific information, so the same overall method can adapt its feature-selection behavior to different tasks.

Feature selection then proceeds through iterative optimization with a closed-form update at each step. This formulation supports direct, efficient optimization of expected test error for features selected from small labeled samples. Experiments show better performance than existing feature-selection methods. The central contribution is to connect learning across tasks with the feature-selection objective itself: the learned kernels are designed to support selections that work well when labels are scarce.
neurips-2022-few-shot-learning-for-featu.tldr: Task-adapted kernels learned across related tasks improve feature selection when only a few labeled examples are available.

paragraphs: Better object-recognition accuracy does not by itself establish that a neural network sees images in a more human-like way. This paper examines two aspects of visual strategy: where people and networks identify important image features, and how they use those features to decide what an object is.

The researchers compare 84 networks trained on ImageNet using three independent datasets of human visual strategies. Across these comparisons, they find a systematic trade-off: networks with higher categorization accuracy are increasingly less aligned with human strategies. This finding concerns the studied models and measurements, and shows why classification accuracy alone is insufficient for judging a network as a model of human vision.

The authors then introduce a general training procedure called the neural harmonizer. It improves alignment between network and human strategies while also improving categorization accuracy. That result matters because it demonstrates that the observed trade-off can be addressed through training. The paper therefore contributes both evidence that prevailing improvements in recognition have moved models away from human behavior and a method for improving the two objectives together.
neurips-2022-harmonizing-the-object-reco.tldr: A study of 84 networks finds an accuracy–human-alignment trade-off and introduces training that improves both.

paragraphs: Many explanations of black-box predictions fit a simple linear model to samples near the input of interest. The paper asks whether those samples cover an appropriate neighborhood. An explanation can be stable across repeated runs while still failing to describe how the original model behaves locally.

Neighborhood size creates a practical tension. Sampling too narrowly can make the fitting problem numerically ill-conditioned and predictions unstable. Sampling too broadly can combine several different linear regions of a nonlinear model, leaving a single linear explanation poorly matched to the input's surroundings. The authors propose an approach that recovers faithful local explanations across different neighborhood widths.

They also develop adaptive neighborhood sampling, or ANS, and formally show that it can require substantially fewer samples and black-box queries than a naive implementation of their approach. Experiments on real data find significant efficiency improvements over competitors while retaining fidelity and stability across widths. The contribution connects explanation quality with sampling design: choosing where to query the model is part of producing a useful local account of its behavior.
neurips-2022-is-this-the-right-neighborh.tldr: Adaptive neighborhood sampling produces faithful, stable local explanations with fewer samples and black-box queries in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Image-captioning models can score well while repeatedly producing generic descriptions. The paper treats this as mode collapse: the model favors a dominant language pattern instead of reflecting the variety present in human captions. Discrete Mode Learning, or DML, aims to learn multiple representative patterns and make them available as explicit controls during generation.

The method has two connected branches. An image-conditioned discrete variational autoencoder assigns captions to embeddings stored in a learned codebook. It uses a non-autoregressive generation objective to encourage distinct, representative modes. A mode-conditioned captioning branch then adds the chosen mode embedding to its word embeddings, allowing an existing captioning model to use the learned pattern as a generation signal.

The authors apply DML to Transformer and AoANet captioning models. On MS COCO, the learned embeddings help these models produce high-quality captions in different modes, improving both diversity and quality. The approach matters because it represents variation within the training captions as something the model can deliberately use, rather than relying on a single dominant description pattern.
neurips-2022-learning-distinct-and-repre.tldr: Discrete Mode Learning gives captioning models learned language-pattern controls that improve caption diversity and quality on MS COCO.

paragraphs: A mixed multinomial logit model combines several logit components to predict probabilities of different outcomes. Learning such a model involves estimating both the relative weight of each component and its own parameters. Although many algorithms already address this problem, the paper focuses on providing theoretical guarantees for the learning process.

The proposed algorithm builds on the Frank-Wolfe optimization method and handles an arbitrary number of mixture components. From historical choice observations, it constructs candidate vectors of choice probabilities that are close to the true probabilities with high probability. The approach learns mixture weights and component-specific parameters within one algorithm, with provable convergence guarantees.

The authors also analyze the amount of data needed and show that a polynomial number of samples suffices for the stated performance guarantee. This adds a statistical requirement alongside the convergence result, addressing both the learning procedure and its data needs. Simulation studies evaluate the method, and the paper demonstrates its application to real-world problems. Its main contribution is a theoretically supported procedure for a mixture-model learning task with previously limited guarantees.
neurips-2022-learning-mixed-multinomial-.tldr: A Frank-Wolfe-based algorithm learns mixed multinomial logit models with convergence guarantees and polynomial sample requirements.

paragraphs: The paper asks why learning features can help some image-classification architectures yet hurt fully connected networks on the same task. Its proposed explanation centers on sparsity. Feature learning can produce a sparser representation, and that representation can generalize worse than approaches based on random features or the neural tangent kernel.

The effect depends on the structure of the target function. Sparsity can be useful for anisotropic data, but the authors show that it can be harmful when the target stays constant or changes smoothly along some input directions. They investigate regression of Gaussian random functions on a multidimensional sphere and calculate how generalization error scales with the number of training examples. In that setting, methods without feature learning generalize better, even in high dimensions.

Experiments on image-classification benchmarks also show that feature learning can create sparse, less smooth predictors. The authors describe this as a plausible explanation for poorer performance, rather than a settled causal account of every case. The findings identify a specific reason representation learning may fail: the learned representation can sacrifice smoothness that the prediction task benefits from preserving.
neurips-2022-learning-sparse-features-ca.tldr: Feature learning can hurt generalization when the sparse representations it produces fail to preserve useful smoothness.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes Thompson Sampling in contextual bandits with binary losses, allowing contexts to be chosen adversarially. Its focus is Bayesian regret, a measure of accumulated decision-making loss averaged under a prior over the unknown model. The challenge is to relate that loss to what the algorithm learns.

The authors modify an information-theoretic analysis by measuring information about the unknown model parameter itself. Earlier approaches in the same setting tracked information about the optimal action or policy. This lifted information ratio yields a simple regret bound in terms of prior entropy, without structural assumptions on the likelihood or prior. Extending the result to priors with infinite entropy requires a Lipschitz condition on the log-likelihood.

For logistic bandits with d-dimensional parameters, K actions, and Lipschitz logits, the resulting upper bound scales as the square root of dKT, up to logarithmic factors. It does not depend on the sigmoid function's smallest slope. The contribution is an analytical perspective that connects uncertainty about model parameters directly to regret, while supporting a useful specialized bound for logistic bandits.
neurips-2022-lifting-the-information-rat.tldr: Tracking information about unknown model parameters yields broad Thompson Sampling regret bounds for contextual bandits with binary losses.

paragraphs: This paper studies a bandit problem in which several agents seek rewarding arms, while the arms also have preferences over agents. The task therefore involves matching participants on two sides of a market. Agents must learn which arms offer higher expected rewards while coordinating their choices with other agents.

A collision occurs when agents select the same arm and can leave them with zero reward. The authors turn this apparent obstacle into a communication mechanism: agents deliberately create collisions to transmit information. They combine the protocol with a layer-based algorithm designed to establish an optimal stable matching between agents and arms. Communication is thus built into the same interactions through which agents obtain rewards.

The resulting decentralized algorithm achieves regret growing on the order of log T, which the abstract reports as state of the art for this matching setting. Experiments also show improvements over existing baselines. The key contribution is the coordination strategy: deliberate collisions provide information that supports learning and matching, even though collisions themselves can sacrifice immediate reward.
neurips-2022-matching-in-multi-arm-bandi.tldr: A collision-based communication protocol supports decentralized stable matching with logarithmic regret.

paragraphs: LIMoE is a sparse mixture-of-experts model that learns from images and text together using a contrastive objective. Its expert layers provide a way for one multimodal backbone to develop different processing behavior for different inputs. The paper explores whether this design can deliver stronger performance at a comparable computational cost.

Training introduces challenges involving stability and balanced use of the experts. The authors propose entropy-based regularization to address them. Their analysis finds different treatment of the two modalities and the emergence of experts specialized for individual modalities, showing how distinct processing can arise within the shared model.

Across several scales, LIMoE improves on dense models with equivalent computational costs. A version trained comparably to CLIP-L/14 reaches 77.9% zero-shot ImageNet accuracy, compared with 76.2%. A larger version trained with additional data reaches 83.8%, approaching leading methods that use separate modality-specific backbones and pretraining schemes. The additional data is part of that scaling result. Together, the findings support sparse expert models as a practical architecture for joint image–text learning.
neurips-2022-multimodal-contrastive-lear.tldr: LIMoE uses a shared sparse expert model for images and text, improving on dense models at equivalent computational cost.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a neural network can represent a scene as individual objects arranged in three-dimensional space. Its goal is to learn decompositions that remain consistent across viewpoints without supervised object labels. Such representations are motivated by the possibility of improving labeled-data efficiency, although the reported contribution centers on learning and rendering the scene decomposition.

Object Scene Representation Transformer, or OSRT, learns through novel-view synthesis: generating a scene's appearance from another viewpoint. Individual object representations emerge through this task within a model organized around three-dimensional scenes. The authors report that OSRT handles substantially more complex scenes, with greater variety in objects and backgrounds, than existing approaches.

The model also uses a light-field parameterization and a Slot Mixer decoder to make compositional rendering multiple orders of magnitude faster. This combines a richer range of representable scenes with a large rendering-speed improvement. The authors see that combination as useful for exploring and scaling future architectures. The work advances a representation-learning approach in which predicting views provides the training signal for discovering separate objects.
neurips-2022-object-scene-representation.tldr: OSRT learns object-based scene representations through novel-view synthesis while supporting more complex scenes and much faster compositional rendering.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can be misled by noisy connections. Some methods address this by learning how strongly information should pass between pairs of nodes, sometimes through multiple propagation channels. The paper argues that these methods often neglect relationships among the messages reaching a node and among the channels, leaving too much freedom to fit the labeled data.

OPEN addresses both kinds of relationships. It models the whole ego-network, the neighborhood centered on a node, to account for how incoming propagations relate to one another. It also imposes diversity across channels. Interpreting propagation as a dimensionality-reduction problem, the method derives weights from mutually orthogonal principal components of the ego-network.

This construction connects propagation weights to the structure of the neighborhood as a whole, rather than treating each pairwise connection independently. Theoretical analysis and experiments support four reported properties: capturing higher-order relationships, preventing overfitting, robustness, and efficiency. The contribution is a structured way to constrain graph propagation so that relationships within neighborhoods and differences between channels both inform how information is combined.
neurips-2022-open-orthogonal-propagation.tldr: OPEN derives graph propagation weights from whole-neighborhood structure and orthogonal components to address noisy topology and overfitting.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning gives different clients distinct local models, helping accommodate differences in their data. Comparing methods is difficult when studies use different datasets, client simulations, implementations, and evaluation protocols. The paper introduces pFL-Bench to make these comparisons more standardized, reproducible, and comprehensive.

The benchmark includes more than ten dataset variants across application areas, with unified data partitioning and realistic heterogeneous settings. A modular codebase supplies more than twenty competitive method implementations and is designed for extension. Evaluations run in containerized environments, providing a common setup for investigating methods whose published results might otherwise be difficult to compare directly.

The evaluation covers generalization, fairness, system overhead, and convergence. The motivation also includes practical questions such as whether a method works for new clients or accommodates participants with limited resources. These concerns broaden assessment beyond performance for the clients already involved in training. The paper highlights the benefits and potential of existing personalized methods, while its main contribution is shared infrastructure for examining their behavior under consistent and practically relevant conditions.
neurips-2022-pfl-bench-a-comprehensive-b.tldr: pFL-Bench standardizes datasets, implementations, and evaluations for comparing personalized federated learning methods under heterogeneous conditions.

paragraphs: Adversarial training is intended to make models robust, yet empirical studies can show a substantial drop in test accuracy compared with ordinary training. This paper starts from the mismatch between that observed degradation and existing theoretical guarantees. It asks whether attack strength changes the behavior of training in a more abrupt way than those guarantees suggest.

The proposed explanation is an asymptotic phase transition. When attacks are small, adversarial training can behave as well as clean training. In a larger-attack regime, the authors propose that a sharp transition occurs. The important distinction is between qualitatively different regimes, rather than assuming that increasing attack strength always produces a similar, gradual change.

The authors validate this conjecture in linear regression models and conduct extensive experiments with deep neural networks. The abstract therefore supports a result in the regression setting alongside an empirical investigation in more complex models. The work offers a way to interpret the gap between favorable theory and degraded performance: conclusions about adversarial training may depend critically on which attack-strength regime is being studied.
neurips-2022-phase-transition-from-clean.tldr: The paper validates an attack-strength-dependent phase transition in linear regression and investigates it experimentally in deep networks.

paragraphs: A social-media post may not contain enough information on its own to classify phenomena such as rumors or sarcasm. The paper explores comments and replies as complementary evidence, capturing how other people discuss the source post. Its model, Hyphen, is designed to use both the post and the hierarchical structure of that surrounding discourse.

Hyphen parses public discussion into an Abstract Meaning Representation graph. It models the graph using hyperbolic geometry, which the approach uses to represent hierarchical relationships. A Fourier co-attention mechanism then captures correlations between the source post and the discussion. This combines a structured representation of public responses with a mechanism for relating those responses to the text being classified.

Experiments cover fake-news, hate-speech, rumor, and sarcasm detection. Hyphen achieves state-of-the-art results across ten benchmark datasets and demonstrates generalization across these tasks. The authors also use sentence-level fact-checked annotations to evaluate explanations that provide evidence associated with the final prediction. The findings support public discourse as a useful additional signal for classification, with the model explicitly representing how that discourse relates to the original post.
neurips-2022-public-wisdom-matters-disco.tldr: Hyphen combines source posts with structured public discussion to improve classification across four social-text tasks.

paragraphs: Squeezeformer revisits the architecture of Conformer, a speech model that combines attention and convolution to capture global and local patterns. Through systematic studies, the authors identify design choices that can be improved. Their changes address both the overall organization of the network and the operations inside individual blocks.

At the larger scale, a Temporal U-Net structure reduces the cost of attention on long sequences. The model also replaces Conformer's Macaron arrangement with simpler blocks in which attention or convolution is followed by a feed-forward module. Within blocks, it simplifies convolutional activations, removes redundant layer-normalization operations, and uses an efficient depthwise layer to reduce the input sequence.

Under the same training schemes, Squeezeformer consistently outperforms the compared leading speech-recognition models. It reports word error rates of 7.5%, 6.5%, and 6.0% on LibriSpeech test-other without external language models, improving on Conformer-CTC at matching FLOP counts. The contribution is an architectural redesign that improves recognition within comparable computational budgets, showing that both high-level structure and smaller operational choices matter for efficiency.
neurips-2022-squeezeformer-an-efficient-.tldr: Squeezeformer improves speech recognition at matched computational cost by redesigning Conformer's sequence structure and internal blocks.

paragraphs: Image restoration should remove degradation wherever it occurs while preserving the local relationships needed to recover a clean image. The paper argues that common transformer attention designs do not adequately respect these requirements. Fixed local windows and global attention can compromise the desired translation behavior and use of local information.

The proposed stochastic window transformer changes how attention windows are placed. During training, it randomly shifts the window partition instead of always using a fixed arrangement. At test time, a layer expectation propagation algorithm efficiently approximates the expected behavior of the resulting stochastic transformer. This provides a practical way to use the randomized design during inference.

The authors report that the approach retains strong representation capabilities while maintaining translation invariance and locality. Experiments show consistent, significant improvements on deraining, denoising, and deblurring. The contribution is a change to the organization of attention that reflects the structure of restoration tasks: image position should not determine whether a degradation is removed, and nearby visual relationships should remain available for reconstructing clean content.
neurips-2022-stochastic-window-transform.tldr: Randomly shifted attention windows and efficient expectation-based inference improve transformer restoration across deraining, denoising, and deblurring.
